panels.rationale: The panel is a panoramic radiograph of a child who has been diagnosed with severe congenital neutropenia. The image clearly demonstrates significant alveolar bone absorption (angular resorption), which is a direct clinical manifestation linked to the disease and the case description.
panels.attribution_text: Tao et al. Oral health management in children with severe congenital neutropenia with periodontitis: Case report.. Medicine 2024. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000039086. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Oral panorama of the child at initial diagnosis. The alveolar bone of the children had different degrees of absorption, and the absorption of the lower anterior teeth was more significant, which was mainly angular resorption.
in_text_mentions: family. Informed consent was obtained from the child parents to allow to be described in this report. Maxillofacial and oral examinations revealed bilateral symmetry of the face and palpable submandibular lymph node enlargement in the neck. The oral hygiene was general, the gums were red and swollen throughout the mouth, the gums were prone to bleeding on probing, the probing depth (PD) was 2 to 7 mm, and the deep periodontal pockets could be probed in some teeth (Figs. 1 and 2). Panoramic radiograph showed that the alveolar ridge of the child was absorbed, showing angular absorption (Fig. 3).

plate_findings.evidence: gingival papillae were soft and dark red with obvious swelling

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A displays the gingival papillae which are soft, dark red, and visibly swollen, consistent with severe periodontitis, a documented complication in severe congenital neutropenia. B: Panel B is a clinical photo of the gingiva exhibiting severe redness and swelling, characteristic of the documented dental manifestations of severe congenital neutropenia. C: Panel C is a clinical photo displaying the patient's oral condition, showing severe gingival inflammation and swelling consistent with the clinical picture of severe congenital neutropenia.

plate_findings.evidence: The roots of the primary teeth were exposed
Panoramic radiography revealed alveolar bone resorption and radiolucencies around the primary molars

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical intraoral photographs demonstrating findings consistent with severe congenital neutropenia, specifically exposed primary tooth roots, observed in an 8-year-old child. B: Panoramic radiograph demonstrating characteristic alveolar bone resorption and radiolucencies, supporting the diagnosis of severe congenital neutropenia.
panels.attribution_text: Akitomo et al. Improvement of Alveolar Bone in a Child with Severe Congenital Neutropenia: Long-Term Clinical Outcomes.. Dentistry journal 2026. doi:10.3390/dj14060355. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Initial examination at the age of 8 years and 5 months. (A) Intraoral photographs. (B) Panoramic radiograph.
in_text_mentions: Nineteen teeth were present in the oral cavity, including three primary second molars (mandibular left primary second molar missing) (Figure 1A). The roots of the primary teeth were exposed, and the teeth had significant mobility, consistent with Miller’s classification as mobility grade II. Additionally, the gingiva around the permanent incisors was red and swollen. Panoramic radiography revealed alveolar bone resorption and radiolucencies around the primary molars (Figure 1B).
